common_name: Gold Rush Dawn Redwood (Golden-Foliaged Dawn Redwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a site with a little afternoon shade in hot inland climates to protect the golden foliage from scorching.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in deep, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun, siting it where a little afternoon shade is available in hot inland climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Gold Rush (also sold as 'Ogon') is a golden-foliaged sport of the species, holding a soft, glowing chartreuse-to-gold color on its feathery, fern-like needles from spring through late summer before fading to tawny orange in fall. It grows more slowly and stays noticeably smaller than seed-grown dawn redwood, developing the same narrowly conical form and shaggy, fibrous, cinnamon-colored bark that makes the species such a striking winter silhouette. Like all dawn redwoods it tolerates wet, seasonally flooded ground as readily as ordinary garden soil, needs no pruning to hold its natural shape, and makes an outstanding specimen or focal-point tree wherever a bright spot of gold foliage color is wanted against a dark background.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of vertical room even though the crown stays narrower than a seed-grown dawn redwood.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing enough vertical room for a large, long-lived tree even though its crown stays narrower than a seed-grown dawn redwood. Selected at the U.S. National Arboretum from the original 1948 Arnold Arboretum seed collection, National is prized for its dense, compact, narrowly conical habit with a strong central leader and unusually dark bark, a much tidier silhouette than the often irregular, wide-spreading form of straight-species trees. It shares the species' fast growth, feathery deciduous foliage that turns coppery orange in fall, and outstanding tolerance of wet or seasonally flooded sites as well as ordinary upland soil. Because its crown stays comparatively narrow at maturity, it fits allees, boulevards, and other spots where a full-sized dawn redwood's spreading form would eventually crowd its neighbors.

common_name: Miss Grace Weeping Dawn Redwood (Dwarf Pendulous Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; stake and train the leader upward for a taller cascading form, or leave unstaked for a low, billowing mound.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Miss Grace was discovered as a witch's-broom mutation and is the first Metasequoia cultivar with a true weeping habit, its soft gray-green needles draped along gracefully pendulous branches that give it a sculptural, almost bonsai-like presence very different from the towering straight species. Left unstaked it forms a low, billowing mound only a few feet tall and wide, while training the leader upright on a stake for the first several years produces a taller, narrower cascading specimen; either way, fall color is a rich orange before the needles drop to reveal attractive peeling bark. Its small mature size makes it a rare option for gardeners who love dawn redwood's texture and history but lack room for a full-sized tree, and it works beautifully as a container specimen, rock garden accent, or small-space focal point.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Saratoga is a grafted male clone selected for slower, denser, more symmetrical branching than many other ginkgo cultivars.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Saratoga is a male ginkgo selection valued for its slower growth rate and dense, symmetrical branching with a strong central leader, giving young trees a tidier look than many faster, more open ginkgo cultivars. Its narrower, somewhat pendulous leaves turn a long-lasting, clear butter-yellow in fall, often holding color after other ginkgo cultivars have already dropped. As a male clone it never bears the malodorous, messy fruit produced by female ginkgo trees, and like all ginkgo it shrugs off urban pollution, compacted soil, heat, and drought once established, with essentially no serious pest or disease problems. Its slower, more restrained growth and refined branching make it a good choice for smaller residential lots or formal plantings where a huge, fast-spreading shade tree would be unwelcome.

common_name: Magyar Ginkgo (Fast-Growing Narrow Pyramidal Male Ginkgo)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Magyar is a grafted male clone selected for faster growth and a uniform narrow-pyramidal habit.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Magyar is a male ginkgo selection prized for its noticeably faster growth and uniform, narrow-pyramidal habit with a strong central leader, reaching landscape size sooner than many other named ginkgo cultivars. Bright green, fan-shaped summer foliage turns a dependable golden yellow in fall. Being a male clone, it never produces the notoriously foul-smelling, messy seeds borne by female ginkgo trees, and mature specimens are exceptionally tough, tolerating urban pollution, heat, compacted soil, and drought with ease once established. Its quicker growth combined with a relatively narrow crown makes it a popular choice for street tree plantings and parking-lot islands where a full canopy is wanted without waiting decades for it to fill in.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun beneath overhead utility lines or in other spots needing a low, broad-crowned shade tree rather than a tall one.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Wireless (cultivar 'Schmidtlow') was selected specifically for its unusually low mature height combined with a broad, horizontally spreading vase form, making it one of the few shade trees suited for planting directly beneath overhead utility lines. Medium green, toothed foliage turns a vivid rusty red in fall, a showier display than many other zelkova selections. It grows quickly for its ultimate size, establishes readily in compacted urban soil, and shares the species' strong resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle. Because its crown stays wide but comparatively short, it is best used along streets and parking areas where overhead clearance is limited rather than as a tall shade tree for open lawns.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous overhead and lateral room for a large, fast-growing shade tree with an upright vase-shaped crown.

directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous overhead and lateral room for a large, fast-growing shade tree. Halka is valued for its vigorous growth and upright, vase-shaped canopy with strong branch attachments, often described as the most American-elm-like of the zelkova cultivars, making it a popular substitute in landscapes that once relied on elms. Fall color is a clear yellow, and mature trees develop attractive gray bark that flakes to reveal orange-brown patches beneath. Like other zelkova selections it tolerates heat, drought, and urban stress once established and resists both Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, needing only structural pruning while young to maintain a single dominant leader.

common_name: City Sprite Zelkova (Compact Semi-Dwarf Selection for Tight Urban Sites)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; its compact semi-dwarf size suits tree lawns, parking islands, and other confined urban sites.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; City Sprite (sold under the patent name 'JFS-KW1') is a compact, semi-dwarf zelkova selection with a tidy, dense, oval-to-vase-shaped crown and finer-textured foliage than the species, staying small enough to fit tree lawns, parking islands, and other confined urban sites where a full-sized zelkova would quickly outgrow its space. Bright green summer leaves turn soft yellow in fall. It shares the species' tolerance of heat, compacted soil, and urban stress along with resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, but needs only minimal structural pruning thanks to its naturally tidy habit. Its restrained mature size makes it one of the better shade tree options for small residential lots and narrow street medians.
sources: Seattle Department of Transportation Urban Forestry

common_name: Prairie Sentinel Pond Cypress (Narrow Columnar Selection)

planting.note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; its exceptionally narrow columnar form fits streets and tight spaces where a wide-spreading conifer would not.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun, though established trees also tolerate ordinary well-drained upland soil. Prairie Sentinel is a strikingly narrow, columnar selection of pond cypress, its stiffly erect branchlets held close to the trunk to form a tight, spire-like silhouette quite unlike the more open, feathery form of typical pond cypress or bald cypress. Its fine, scale-like foliage is bright green through the growing season, turning rich russet-brown before dropping in fall, and like the species it develops picturesque knees in consistently wet ground while also thriving in drier upland plantings. Its exceptionally narrow mature width makes it a good choice for street trees, screening, or accent plantings in tight spaces where a wide-spreading conifer would not fit.

common_name: Lindsey's Skyward Bald Cypress (Dwarf Columnar Selection with Upswept Branches)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; this naturally dwarf, extremely narrow selection needs no staking to hold its dense, upright columnar form.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lindsey's Skyward is a naturally dwarf, extremely narrow bald cypress selection discovered as a chance seedling mutation, its branches ascending stiffly upward and tightly to the trunk rather than spreading outward, forming a dense, columnar silhouette from the ground to the tip even without staking or pruning. Soft, feathery green needles turn a warm coppery orange in fall, and the textured, bronze-toned bark adds interest through winter once the foliage has dropped. Unlike most bald cypress, its slow growth and diminutive footprint suit small residential yards, narrow side-yard plantings, and container culture, though it retains the species' tolerance for both occasionally wet soil and ordinary garden conditions once established. Little maintenance is needed beyond removing any wayward shoot that departs from its naturally tight, upright form.
sources: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office Plant Patent PP22,812
